slides.headline: Most exit doors push outward because of one Boston nightclub

image.credit: Photo: Cocoanut Grove Memorial, Boston / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5

slides.text: On November 28, 1942, fire swept Boston's Cocoanut Grove nightclub. About 1,000 people were inside a club rated for 460. The main exit was one revolving door, and it jammed. 492 died.

image.credit: City of Boston Fire Department, Report concerning the Cocoanut Grove Fire (1943) / Internet Archive, public domain

slides.text: Side doors were bolted shut. Other exits opened inward, so the crowd pressed them closed. Fire officials later testified that outward-swinging doors could have saved at least 300 lives.
Boston rewrote its fire rules and many states followed: exit doors that open outward, exit signs always visible, no flammable decor, and revolving doors flanked by regular doors or able to fold flat.

image.credit: First-floor plan, City of Boston Fire Department, Report concerning the Cocoanut Grove Fire (1943) / Internet Archive, public domain

slides.text: Next time you push an exit door open without thinking, you're using a rule written in 1942.

caption:
Push an exit door and it swings out. That is not an accident of design.

On November 28, 1942, a fire tore through the Cocoanut Grove nightclub in Boston. It killed 492 people and remains the deadliest nightclub fire in U.S. history. Around 1,000 guests were inside a club with an official capacity of 460.

The main entrance was one revolving door, which jammed under the crush of the crowd. Some side doors were bolted shut, a window was boarded up, and other doors opened inward, so the crowd itself held them closed. The club had no sprinklers, and flammable paper palm trees and drapes helped the fire spread. Fire officials testified that outward-swinging doors could have saved at least 300 lives.

In the years afterward, Boston overhauled its building codes and many states passed laws: no inward-swinging exit doors, exit signs visible at all times, a ban on flammable decorations, sprinklers for places like restaurants and clubs, and revolving doors flanked by normal outward-swinging doors or built to fold flat. Massachusetts also created a statewide fire code.

The cause is still debated, but the rules came from what trapped people.

Source: Fire Fighter Nation; NBC Boston.
